proposal.problem: On every project the contractor submits an updated programme, a Primavera P6 or MS Project schedule, and a planning engineer of the project management firm has to review it before the project manager can accept it on the employer's behalf. Today this review is done by eye: the engineer filters the activity table, looks for activities without predecessors or successors, hard constraints, negative float and unexplained lags, and writes the comments into an e-mail or a spreadsheet by hand. The DCMA 14-point assessment is the common yardstick for schedule quality: for example, at most 5% of incomplete activities may miss a predecessor or successor, no link may have a negative lag, and at most 5% of activities may carry more than 44 working days of total float. Counting these by hand across a large programme is slow and error-prone, and two engineers rarely count the same way; even the commercial tools that automate the checks are not certified and count activities differently. When a defective programme is accepted, its critical path is wrong, and every later delay or extension-of-time discussion rests on a schedule nobody fully checked.
proposal.mission: Help the planning engineers of a construction project management firm review contractor programmes faster and more consistently. The project delivers a Python tool that reads a programme exported to Excel, checks it against twelve of the DCMA 14-point schedule quality checks written as SHACL rules, and produces an Excel report that lists every finding by activity. With this report, the planning engineer can send precise, rule-based comments to the contractor, and the project manager can accept a programme knowing that its logic, float and dates have been checked the same way every time.
proposal.outcome: A planning engineer runs one command on the contractor's exported programme and, within a minute, receives an Excel report with a pass or fail for twelve DCMA checks and a list of every offending activity, ready to send back to the contractor, instead of filtering the schedule by hand.

proposal.techWhy: RDFLib turns the rows of the Excel template into RDF statements about the project, its activities and the relationships between them, so that each finding can point at the activity or link it concerns. SHACL shapes, run by pySHACL, hold the eleven rule-based DCMA checks; each threshold is a value in the shapes file, so a planning engineer can change it without touching code. SPARQL queries count the ratios each check is judged by and compute the baseline execution index for the report's summary sheet.

proposal.spec: The tool reads a programme from the three-sheet Excel template (Project, Activities, Relationships), refuses a file whose required columns are missing and names them, and converts each value, accepting forms such as 12, 12d or 12 gün. It maps the programme to an RDF graph and validates it with SHACL shapes for checks 1 to 11 of the DCMA 14-point assessment; SPARQL queries compute each check's ratio and the baseline execution index. It writes an Excel report with a summary sheet (value, threshold and pass, fail or not applicable per check), a findings sheet with one row per finding, and a method sheet with the counting rules. Given a folder, it checks every file in parallel and adds one summary table. It never recalculates the schedule and never sends data outside the computer.

scenarios.text: Given a defect-free synthetic programme of 200 activities, when the planning engineer runs the checker, then all twelve checks pass and the findings sheet is empty
Given a template whose Relationships sheet lacks the predecessor column, when the checker reads it, then it stops, names the missing column and writes no report
Given an activity with exactly 44 working days of total float, when the checker runs, then check 6 reports no finding for it, and at 45 days it does
Given a programme with an empty baseline finish column, when the checker runs, then checks 11 and 14 are reported as not applicable rather than passed

proposal.activity: The planning engineer exports the contractor's programme to the template and starts the checker on a file or a folder. For a folder, each file is processed in its own thread. The reader opens the workbook; if a required sheet or column is missing it stops and reports it. Otherwise it cleans each value, and an unreadable cell is reported with its sheet and row. The rows are mapped to an RDF graph. pySHACL validates the graph against the shapes and SPARQL queries compute the ratios and the baseline execution index; if the baseline column is empty, checks 11 and 14 are marked not applicable. The report writer produces the Excel report, and for a folder the summary table.
proposal.sequence: The planning engineer calls the command-line tool with a path. The tool asks the Reader for the three sheets and receives rows or a list of missing columns. It sends the rows to the Mapper, which returns an RDF graph. It sends the graph and the shapes file to the Validator (pySHACL), which returns the validation report. It sends the graph to the Metrics module, which runs the SPARQL queries and returns one value per check. It passes the findings and values to the ReportWriter, which writes the Excel file and returns its path, and the tool prints the path for the engineer.

proposal.classModel: Project has a name and a data date and has many Activities. Activity has an id, name, type (task, milestone, level of effort, summary), status, duration, start, finish, actual start, actual finish, total float, constraint type, baseline finish and resource. Relationship links a predecessor Activity to a successor Activity and has a type (FS, SS, FF, SF) and a lag. Check has a number, a name, a threshold and a counting rule. Finding links one Check to one Activity or Relationship and has a measured value and a message. AuditReport belongs to one Project and holds a result per Check and many Findings.

proposal.model_Data: Class diagram: Project, Activity, Relationship, Check, Finding and AuditReport as in the class model. SHACL node shapes target Activity and Relationship, one shape per check, each with its threshold as a parameter and a message for the report.
proposal.model_Interface: Component diagram: the CLI calls the Reader (openpyxl, re), which feeds the Mapper (RDFLib); the Validator (pySHACL) reads the graph and the shapes file; Metrics runs the SPARQL queries; the ReportWriter (openpyxl) writes the Excel report. The file contracts are the three-sheet input template and the three-sheet report.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sequence diagram: the planning engineer runs the command with a file or folder path; the tool prints progress per file and then the report path, or the missing column and stops; the project manager opens the report and reads the summary sheet.
proposal.libraries: openpyxl reads the Excel template and writes the audit report, regular expressions clean values such as 12d or 12 gün and check activity id patterns, pathlib walks a folder of programmes and stores the reports, and a thread pool checks several files in parallel. RDFLib builds the graph, pySHACL validates it against the shapes and pytest runs the tests. The project applies the course's spreadsheet, regular expressions, files and paths, and multithreading chapters.
